name: Marco Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep sixteen thousand free-range laying hens in two flocks, plus a hundred acres of wheat that I sell and some grass the hens range on. First thing, around six, I check the overnight numbers on my phone: water use, shed temperature, how many eggs came down the belt. If water's down, something's wrong, maybe a blocked drinker line, maybe the birds are getting sick. Then I walk both sheds, because the numbers tell you something's wrong but not what.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the data, honestly, and I love opening the pop-holes in the morning and watching eight thousand hens pour out onto the grass like water. What wears me out is bird flu. Every autumn we're waiting for the letter that says keep them all inside, and one year we lost a whole flock to it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ana, my wife, is a social worker, so she's not on the farm much, but she does the egg rounds on Saturdays for our little box scheme. I've got two full-time staff, Leon and Bea, and a couple of locals for packing. Our son's an engineer abroad, and our daughter teaches primary school an hour away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI tools now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it about feed costs, I get it to read the bird health reports and tell me what changed since last week, and I used it to write our flock plan for the inspector. It's wrong sometimes, so I treat it like a bright new worker. Check everything, but don't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and anyone who's not trying it is missing a trick. I've told half the poultry group that. Some of them look at me like I've grown a second head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, if it stays just a tool, that's honestly a bit disappointing. I'd hoped for something that could help spot disease earlier. But nothing changes for my staff, so that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it daily, try it on the grain selling side, which I'm bad at. Spend maybe two thousand on better sensors in the sheds so it has more to read. Run a short session for the poultry group at the village hall, show them what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I'm excited about this stuff and here it is, staying ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you run a session for the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the small farms get left behind every time. The big integrators, the companies that own the birds and the feed and the contracts, they'll have all of this. If small farmers don't learn it, they'll be squeezed even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the egg packer started using it against us. Say they had software that worked out the lowest price each farm would accept. That's when it becomes their tool, not mine. Then I'd want rules.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, and anyone not trying it is missing a trick. I've told half the poultry group that, and some look at me like I've grown a second head.
S0.think: If it stays just a tool, that's a bit disappointing, because I'd hoped it would spot disease earlier. But nothing changes for my staff, so that's fine.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and tries it on grain selling. Spends about two thousand on more shed sensors and runs a short session at the village hall to show the poultry group what he does.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, since he's excited by the technology and it stays ordinary.
S0.quote: If small farmers don't learn it, they'll be squeezed even harder.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the rare farmer who is mildly let down that nothing changes. His politics show in his worry that big integrators will get the tools first. His line in the sand is the egg packer using AI against farmers on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine for most people but small farms shouldn't wait ten years. And companies hiring fewer beginners is a mistake. Who'll know how to fix anything in fifteen years if nobody learns now?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm already ahead, and slow means I get a long head start. The bit I don't like is Bea. She's twenty-six and she's my best stockperson. If the job market for young people shrinks, she's stuck, and she's ambitious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a disease warning system as soon as there's one that works, probably within the year. Pay for Bea to do a poultry management course, around fifteen hundred. Start talking to two neighbours about sharing kit and data, a sort of small co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. Slightly uneasy that the long head start is only for people like me who already like this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the co-op idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three egg farms within ten miles, all about my size. If we pooled our data and bought the expensive systems together, we'd be as clever as one big integrator. Gwen next door would hate the word co-op, mind you. I'd call it a buying group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow suits you because you're ahead. Is that fair on the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it isn't, and that bothers me. It's like broadband all over again. The farms near the main road got it first and the hill farms waited years. I'd want public money for training so it isn't just the keen ones who benefit.

S1.say: Slow is fine for most people, but small farms shouldn't wait ten years. Hiring fewer beginners is a mistake, because nobody will know how to fix anything in fifteen years.
S1.think: Honestly, it's good for me, because I'm already ahead and slow gives me a long head start. I don't like what it means for Bea, my best stockperson, who's young and ambitious.
S1.do: Buys a disease early warning system within the year and pays about fifteen hundred for Bea's poultry management course. Starts talks with two neighbouring egg farms about pooling data and buying kit together.
S1.feel: Mostly hopeful, with some unease that the head start only goes to people who already like this technology.
S1.quote: It's like broadband all over again. The farms near the main road got it first and the hill farms waited years.
S1.fieldNote: He is candid that slow spread benefits him, and then questions whether that's fair. The co-op idea is his progressive politics turned into a practical plan. He is ready to rename it to get a traditional neighbour on board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should make the companies that cut office jobs pay for retraining, and quickly. And I'd say farmers who think this is someone else's problem should look at who buys their eggs. Office workers stop buying free-range when they're scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be using those assistants to run my whole farm office. Contracts, staff rotas, the inspection paperwork. It could save me ten hours a week. I'd just feel sick about the people in the egg packer's office who'd lose their jobs doing the same work for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up an assistant on the farm office within the first three months. Use the saved time to grow the box scheme from sixty customers to two hundred, because local customers are safer than the packer. And talk to Ana about what she's seeing, because social workers see the layoffs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at the same time. It's like a new tractor that does more than you need, and you can't stop thinking about the people who used to do it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the box scheme be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if people are losing office jobs, the supermarkets will push for cheaper eggs, and the packer will push that onto me. But my box customers know my hens. Some of them visit. They'll pay forty pence more a dozen for that, at least I hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm being naive. She'd say the people losing jobs won't be buying my eggs at any price, they'll be at the food bank. She's probably right. I'd still try it.

S2.say: The government should make companies that cut office jobs pay for retraining, quickly. Farmers who think it's someone else's problem should remember scared office workers stop buying free-range eggs.
S2.think: I'd use the assistants to run my whole farm office and save ten hours a week. I'd feel sick about the people in the egg packer's office who'd lose their jobs doing the same work.
S2.do: Sets up an AI assistant for the farm office within three months. Uses the saved time to grow the egg box scheme from sixty customers to two hundred and talks with his wife about what she sees as a social worker.
S2.feel: Excited and uneasy at once, aware of the people who used to do the work by hand.
S2.quote: My box customers know my hens. Some of them visit.
S2.fieldNote: He sees the knock-on effect on egg demand straight away, which most farmers wouldn't. His answer is to get closer to his customers rather than the packer. His wife plays the sceptic in his head, and he accepts she may be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a political crisis because it's a fairness crisis. If AI makes a few people very rich, then public ownership of some of it, or a big tax, has to be on the table. I'd go to the rallies and I'd say it on the poultry group chat, which would cause a row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Physical work is untouched, my land's up, and my skills are suddenly useful because I know the tech. But my son's an engineer. If AI matches skilled professionals, his job's in it too, and he's got two kids abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring Danny and tell him to save hard and keep an eye out. Offer to help with school fees for the grandkids if he needs it, maybe five thousand a year. Keep the farm steady, no big spending, because when share prices boom like that they usually crash afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for Danny. It's strange, because for once the farmer is the safe one in the family. I'd feel lucky and guilty in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Danny on that call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That his dad has sixteen thousand hens that don't care about AI and there's always a job collecting eggs. He'd laugh. Then I'd tell him seriously to learn the tools faster than anyone around him, because that's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said booms usually crash. What's that based on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was thirty when the last big crash hit. Feed prices went mad, two neighbours went bust, and I nearly did. I learned then not to buy a new shed when everyone's feeling rich.

S3.say: It's a political crisis because it's a fairness crisis. If AI makes a few people very rich, public ownership or a big tax has to be on the table.
S3.think: I'd be fine, with physical work untouched, my land up and my tech skills suddenly useful. But my son Danny is an engineer abroad with two kids, and his job is in it too.
S3.do: Calls his son to tell him to save hard and learn the tools fast. Offers about five thousand a year towards the grandchildren's school fees and keeps the farm steady with no big spending, expecting a crash after the boom.
S3.feel: Worried for his son, and both lucky and guilty that the farmer is the safe one in the family.
S3.quote: For once the farmer is the safe one in the family. I'd feel lucky and guilty in the same breath.
S3.fieldNote: The role reversal, with the farmer as the secure one, clearly moves him. His caution about booms comes from surviving a crash at thirty, and it balances his love of new things. His left-leaning views get louder here, including public ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms could be good if farmers and workers own them and share the gains, and terrible if the integrators own them. I'd be pushing hard for co-ops and for a law that protects workers' wages during the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd probably be one of the first to buy an egg-collecting robot. I'd be fascinated. But Leon is fifty-five and he's done this all his life. Bea could retrain. Leon, I'm not so sure. That's the part I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at a robot that walks the sheds and picks up floor eggs, and trial one in the first year, maybe twenty thousand on a lease. Guarantee Leon's job until he's sixty, written into his contract. Get the buying group to bargain together for robots so the integrators don't set the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thrilled and scared. Thrilled because I've dreamed about this, scared because the dream comes with Leon's face on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leon on the day the robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's going to be its boss. That's not a joke, someone has to watch it and fix it and know when it's wrong. Leon knows when a hen's sick by the way she stands. A robot won't know that for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy one early. Would that put pressure on your neighbours to follow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it would. If I can sell eggs a few pence cheaper, Gwen next door has to match me or lose her contract. I've thought about that. It's why I want the buying group first, so we all move together instead of picking each other off.

S4.say: Robots on farms could be good if farmers and workers own them and share the gains, and terrible if the integrators own them. I'd push hard for co-ops and wage protection.
S4.think: I'd probably be one of the first to buy an egg-collecting robot, because it fascinates me. But Leon is fifty-five and has done this all his life, and that's what I'd lose sleep over.
S4.do: Trials a shed-walking egg-collecting robot on a lease of about twenty thousand in the first year. Writes Leon's job guarantee until sixty into his contract and gets the buying group to bargain for robots together.
S4.feel: Thrilled and scared at once, because the thing he's dreamed of comes with his worker's face on it.
S4.quote: Thrilled because I've dreamed about this, scared because the dream comes with Leon's face on it.
S4.fieldNote: Even here he stays in control, which is why mood is anxious rather than alarmed. He sees that being an early mover would push neighbours into a race, and he plans the buying group to stop it. His loyalty to Leon is specific and practical.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because it's the one where I could hurt people I care about just by being myself. What would help is public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together, and wage protection for workers like Leon while they move into new roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the data. Every robot and sensor sends numbers somewhere. If the integrator owns my flock data, they know my costs better than I do. I'd want a law that says the farmer owns what the farm produces, numbers included.

headlineQuote: Thrilled because I've dreamed about this, scared because the dream comes with Leon's face on it.
portrait: Marco Reyes is fifty-eight and keeps sixteen thousand free-range hens and some wheat, and he checks his flock data on his phone before he's out of bed. He uses AI every day and is mildly disappointed when it stays ordinary. His left-leaning views turn into practical plans: a buying group with neighbours, a bigger box scheme, public ownership talk when the gains go to the few. The fast pictures make him the safe one in his family, which leaves him lucky and guilty. In the robot picture he would buy early but bind himself to protect his worker Leon and avoid a race with his neighbours.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because by being an early adopter he could hurt people he cares about, especially his worker Leon and the farm next door.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together, wage protection for workers moving into new roles, and a law that farmers own their farm data.
